entries.name: The Estate of Ewell E. Long v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: "But-for" nexus under 10 Del. C. § 3104(c)(1)-(3): rejected. The Long-Arm Statute requires that the act be a "source" of the claim, not a but-for cause. Under LVI, executing the form did not itself effect collection of the death benefit, and Wells Fargo and Perlino took no part in the 2007 procurement.

Conspiracy theory of jurisdiction: rejected on the first two Istituto Bancario elements. Wells Fargo and Perlino could have had a meeting of the minds only if they knew the Policy was an illegal wager rather than a legal secondary-market policy. The knowledge allegations were conclusory or on information and belief, and nothing suggested the 2020 purchase was other than arm's-length or that Defendants acted on the prior owners' behalf, at their direction, or for their benefit.

Section 3104(c)(4) is not coextensive with Daimler: rejected. Subsection (c)(4) is "canonized as the general jurisdiction statute," so the result is the same whether Daimler limits (c)(4) or applies as a separate due process step. Plaintiff's cases (LaNuova, Round Rock) predate Daimler.

Section 3104(c)(3) tortious injury: rejected. No breach of a duty to anyone was alleged, because a § 2704(b) claim is not based on a violation of the claimant's rights. Any injury likely would have been felt in Florida.

Alter ego jurisdiction through Jade Mountain: abandoned and waived. Plaintiff did not respond after Defendants showed, through Jade Mountain's SEC filings, that it owns about 0% of Perlino and lacks discretionary authority over it (fn. 94).

Estate of Oristano bench ruling sustaining a STOLI conspiracy claim: not followed. That ruling did not squarely address whether secondary liability exists under § 2704(b), and it did not address Frank.

Distinguishing Edgewater because DUFTA derives from a uniform act: rejected. The uniform-act point was additional, not necessary, support, and the reasoning that statutory causes of action do not carry implied secondary liability applies equally to § 2704(b) (fn. 190).

Refusing secondary liability would gut the insurable-interest regime: rejected. Section 2704(b) reaches "any" beneficiary or other payee that received benefits, including transferees, and insurers may refuse payment under § 2704(a). Any expansion is for the General Assembly.

Conspiracy claim broader than a § 2704(b) violation: rejected. No facts were pled supporting an emotional distress or invasion of privacy tort, and Plaintiff did not argue that a private right of action exists to enforce § 2704(a) or secondary liability under it (fn. 197).
Edwards v. Concord EFS (conspiracy based on Title VII and § 1981): distinguished. Those statutes remedy violations of the plaintiff's private rights, whereas § 2704(b) does not.

authorities_cited.proposition: Subsection (a) codifies the insurable-interest requirement. Subsection (b) gives the insured or executor an action to recover benefits from the beneficiary, assignee or other payee "so receiving them." The statute defines who may sue, against whom, and for what remedy, and says nothing of secondary liability.

Subsections (c)(1)-(3) confer specific jurisdiction only over claims "arising from" the enumerated Delaware acts. Subsection (c)(3) requires both a Delaware act and a tortious injury in Delaware. Subsection (c)(4) confers general jurisdiction.

authorities_cited.authority: GWG DLP Master Tr. v. Est. of Frank, 361 A.3d 31 (Del. 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: An estate's right to recover a STOLI death benefit did not exist at common law. It is a statutorily created "new right" under § 2704(b), and estates have other tools against STOLI actors.

authorities_cited.authority: Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v. Est. of Malkin, 278 A.3d 53 (Del. 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: STOLI policies are void ab initio. A § 2704(b) claim rests on violation of the Delaware Constitution and public policy, not on a "violation of the rights of the claimant."

authorities_cited.authority: PHL Variable Ins. Co. v. Price Dawe 2006 Ins. Tr., 28 A.3d 1059 (Del. 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Insurable interest is tested at inception. The secondary market is legal, and STOLI status turns on who in fact procured the policy, so knowledge that a policy is an illegal wager is not obvious.

authorities_cited.authority: Lavastone Cap. LLC v. Est. of Berland, 266 A.3d 964 (Del. 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: Section 2704(b) lets the estate recover the death benefit from the recipient. Nonrecourse premium funding is not dispositive of STOLI status.

authorities_cited.authority: LVI Grp. Invs., LLC v. NCM Grp. Hldgs., LLC, 2017 WL 3912632 (Del. Ch. Sept. 7, 2017)
authorities_cited.proposition: The Long-Arm Statute's nexus requires that the Delaware act form a source of the claim. An antecedent act that did not itself effect the challenged transaction is insufficient.

authorities_cited.authority: Est. of Daher v. LSH CO., 2021 WL 184394 (D. Del. Jan. 19, 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: A downstream purchaser of an alleged STOLI is not subject to long-arm jurisdiction merely because the policy is governed by Delaware law or was held by Delaware entities. Conspiracy jurisdiction fails absent non-conclusory allegations of the purchaser's involvement in procurement or a meeting of the minds.

authorities_cited.authority: Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 117 (2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: General jurisdiction over a foreign entity requires affiliations so continuous and systematic as to render it essentially at home in the forum.

authorities_cited.authority: Istituto Bancario Italiano SpA v. Hunter Eng'g Co., 449 A.2d 210 (Del. 1982)
authorities_cited.proposition: Five-element conspiracy theory of jurisdiction; it is a strict test.

authorities_cited.authority: Edgewater Growth Cap. P'rs, L.P. v. H.I.G. Cap., Inc., 2010 WL 720150 (Del. Ch. Mar. 3, 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: No implied aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy claim exists under a statute (DUFTA) that specifies the parties liable and the remedies; creating one is for the General Assembly.

authorities_cited.authority: SpecialtyCare, Inc. v. MedCost, LLC, 2026 WL 432302 (Del. Ch. Feb. 16, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Where a statute expressly provides particular remedies, a court must be chary of reading others into it.

authorities_cited.authority: Reylek v. Albence, 2023 WL 8850074 (Del. Super. Dec. 21, 2023); Rays Plumbing & Heating Serv., Inc. v. Stover Homes, L.L.C., 2011 WL 3329384 (Del. Super. July 26, 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Implied private remedies require strong evidence of legislative intent; Delaware tracks federal law on implied rights of action.

authorities_cited.authority: Edwards v. GigAcquisitions2, LLC, 2025 WL 2092832 (Del. Ch. July 25, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Allegations resting solely on information and belief do not satisfy the conspiracy-jurisdiction showing.

authorities_cited.authority: Hercules Inc. v. Leu Tr. & Banking (Bah.) Ltd., 611 A.2d 476 (Del. 1992)
authorities_cited.proposition: Jurisdictional agency includes co-conspirators; conspiracy jurisdiction rests on agency principles.

authorities_cited.authority: Restatement (Third) of Agency §§ 1.01, 8.01
authorities_cited.proposition: An agent acts on the principal's behalf, subject to its control and for its benefit.

authorities_cited.authority: Ultragenyx Pharm., Inc. v. Catalent Md., Inc., 2025 WL 4667818 (Del. Super. Dec. 16, 2025); VTB Bank v. Navitron Projects Corp., 2014 WL 1691250 (Del. Ch. Apr. 28, 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: Failure to brief a jurisdictional theory waives it.

authorities_cited.authority: Genuine Parts Co. v. Cepec, 137 A.3d 123 (Del. 2016)
authorities_cited.proposition: General jurisdiction permits suit on any claim; it requires being at home in the forum.

authorities_cited.authority: NACCO Indus., Inc. v. Applica Inc., 997 A.2d 1 (Del. Ch. 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Its statement that a conspiracy may rest on a "statutory violation" was not a holding that any statutory cause of action supports conspiracy; no statutory violation was at issue there.

authorities_cited.authority: Am. Gen. Life Ins. v. Goldstein, 741 F. Supp. 2d 604 (D. Del. 2010); Ohio Nat'l Life Assurance Corp. v. Davis, 13 F. Supp. 3d 876 (N.D. Ill. 2014)
authorities_cited.proposition: Both were insurer suits; Goldstein's conspiracy claim rested on intentional misrepresentation, and Davis applied Illinois law, which lacks an analogue to § 2704(b).

authorities_cited.authority: Est. of Oristano v. Westgate Del. LLC, C.A. No. N23C-04-258 EMD CCLD (Del. Super. June 18, 2026) (TRANSCRIPT)
authorities_cited.proposition: Its bench ruling sustaining a STOLI conspiracy claim did not squarely address whether secondary liability exists under § 2704(b) and did not address Frank.

authorities_cited.authority: Rule 12(b)(2); Rule 12(b)(6)
authorities_cited.proposition: Dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction and for failure to state a claim.

summary.brief_summary: The Estate of Ewell E. Long sued Perlino, the downstream purchaser of an alleged STOLI Policy, its securities intermediary Wells Fargo, and investment advisor Jade Mountain to recover the death benefit under 18 Del. C. § 2704(b), adding civil conspiracy and aiding-and-abetting counts; Defendants moved to dismiss the amended complaint under Rules 12(b)(2) and 12(b)(6). The Court held that Wells Fargo's Delaware signing of a change-in-beneficiary form was not a "source" of the § 2704(b) claim, that neither foreign defendant was at home in Delaware, and that conspiracy jurisdiction failed for lack of specific facts showing the downstream buyers knew the Policy was an illegal wager. Relying on Frank's holding that the estate's recovery right is a statutory creation, and on Edgewater, the Court held that § 2704(b) carries no implied secondary liability against non-recipients such as Jade Mountain.
summary.core_legal_issue: Two questions. First, whether the Superior Court has personal jurisdiction over Wells Fargo and Perlino, a foreign securities intermediary and the downstream purchaser of an alleged STOLI Policy, where their only alleged Delaware act was Wells Fargo's execution in Delaware of a change-of-owner-and-beneficiary form. Second, whether 18 Del. C. § 2704(b) supports claims for civil conspiracy or aiding and abetting a wager on human life against Jade Mountain, an investment advisor that did not receive the death benefit.
summary.holding: Motion granted. Under Rule 12(b)(2), the claims against Wells Fargo and Perlino are dismissed without prejudice to Plaintiff's right to assert them in a court of competent jurisdiction. Because a § 2704(b) claim is a creature of statute, its "sources" are the procurement of a policy lacking an insurable interest and, arguably, the collection of the death benefit. Wells Fargo's Delaware execution of the change-in-beneficiary form was neither, because procurement occurred 13 years earlier without these Defendants and collection occurred in Minnesota. A but-for connection is insufficient. Section 3104(c)(3) also failed because no tortious injury was pled. General jurisdiction under (c)(4) failed under Daimler. Conspiracy jurisdiction failed for lack of specific facts showing a meeting of the minds or membership, and because the arm's-length relationship with prior owners could not be stretched into agency. Under Rule 12(b)(6), the conspiracy and aiding-and-abetting counts against Jade Mountain are dismissed with prejudice. Section 2704(b) expressly defines who may sue, the recipients who may be sued, and the remedy, so the Court would not imply secondary liability against non-recipients seeking additional damages, particularly after Frank held the right is new rather than codified common law. The Court did not reach: whether the form signing was a ministerial or de minimis act (fn. 125); Defendants' additional conspiracy-jurisdiction arguments (fn. 169); Defendants' due process arguments (fn. 170); Defendants' remaining arguments against Counts II and III; or Florida law (fn. 212).
key_facts_and_concessions: The only Delaware act identified by Plaintiff was Wells Fargo's execution in Delaware, through an Assistant Vice President, of a "Change of Non-Individual Owner and Beneficiary Form" in 2020; WSFS also signed the form in Delaware.
The undisputed record shows that Wells Fargo received the death benefit from the insurer in March 2022 and credited it to Perlino's account in Minnesota.

The Policy was procured in 2007 through Ocean Gate. Perlino was formed in May 2020 and acquired the Policy in June 2020. Plaintiff did not dispute that Defendants were not involved at the Policy's inception (fn. 154).
Wells Fargo is a South Dakota citizen and Perlino is a Florida LP with its principal place of business in Texas. Plaintiff did not argue that Daimler's "essentially at home" test was satisfied.

Allegations that Wells Fargo and Perlino knew the Policy was an illegal wager were conclusory. The allegation that Perlino had data-room access to the Policy documents was pled "[u]pon information and belief," and Wells Fargo was not alleged to have had such access at all (fn. 158).
Count I (recovery of proceeds) was asserted only against Wells Fargo and Perlino. Jade Mountain faced only the conspiracy and aiding-and-abetting counts and did not receive the death benefit.
Plaintiff's secondary-liability counts sought damages beyond the death benefit, for "dignitary and emotional harm" and intrusion on Long's privacy.
Plaintiff confirmed its Florida law arguments were made only if Delaware law did not apply. No party argued against Delaware law, so the Court applied Delaware law (fn. 212).
summary.practical_takeaway: Estates pursuing STOLI proceeds should sue the recipients and transferees of the death benefit directly under § 2704(b), in a forum where those defendants are at home or where procurement or collection occurred. Conspiracy or aiding-and-abetting counts against non-recipient advisors will not survive in Delaware. Anyone invoking conspiracy jurisdiction over downstream purchasers needs specific, non-information-and-belief facts showing that they knew the policy was an illegal wager, not merely that they bought it on the secondary market.
summary.standard_of_review: Rule 12(b)(2): Plaintiff bears the burden to show a statutory basis for service and that jurisdiction comports with due process, as to each defendant. With no evidentiary hearing, a prima facie showing suffices, the record is construed in Plaintiff's favor, and allegations are accepted unless contradicted by affidavit. Conspiracy jurisdiction is a "strict test" requiring specific factual evidence, not conclusory allegations. Rule 12(b)(6): reasonable conceivability; conclusory allegations and unreasonable inferences are not credited.

entries.name: Joseph W. C. Murray, Jr., et al. v. Nikola Preradovic, et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Preradovics' argument that subdividing the disputed area was error: no legal error, because Justice v. McGinn and out-of-state common law authority permit awarding title only to the portion where the elements are met. The Court nonetheless declined to subdivide as a factual matter because the area forms a physically cohesive whole and the Murrays proved every element as to all of it, which defeats the Preradovics' aim of denying any award.

Preradovics' argument that the Murrays failed to establish the elements of adverse possession even for the fenced area: rejected; the fence "easily" satisfies continuity and makes possession obvious, hostile and exclusive.
Preradovics' exception that the Magistrate relied on improper or speculative testimony: resolved by the Court citing only record portions containing competent evidence (fn. 113).

Preradovics' argument that possession was not open and notorious because Zeljka never saw the Murrays maintaining the planter on neighborhood walks: rejected; constant presence is not how owners use a backyard and is not required, and the trimmed ivy, controlled bamboo and mowed grass would have been obvious to an observer.

The Magistrate's conclusion that overgrown ivy showed diminished, non-continuous maintenance of the planter: rejected; the law does not require meticulously manicured landscaping, the photographs show trimmed ivy and mowed grass, and there was no abandonment or exclusion between 1998 and 2018.

The Magistrate's conclusion that mowing the grass strip does not communicate ownership and that others' access defeated exclusivity and hostility: rejected. Until late 2022, residents of 234 South Dillwyn did not use the planter or mow around it, and the Murrays maintained the features marking the practical boundary.

Late-2022 maintenance by the Preradovics as an interruption: rejected as immaterial, because any interruption came after twenty years of continuous possession and title once acquired is not lost by a later break in possession.

authorities_cited.proposition: Codifies the common law cause of action for adverse possession.

authorities_cited.authority: Justice v. McGinn, 2001 WL 1088760 (Del. Ch. Aug. 29, 2001)
authorities_cited.proposition: This court has subdivided a disputed tract and entered adverse possession judgment only for the portion where the elements were met, so the Magistrate's subdivision was not legal error.

authorities_cited.authority: Tumulty v. Schreppler, 132 A.3d 4 (Del. Ch. 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Sets out the elements of adverse possession (continuous for twenty years, open and notorious, hostile and adverse, exclusive, actual) and the preponderance burden; defines open and notorious and exclusive possession; actual possession largely overlaps with open and notorious possession.

authorities_cited.authority: Lewes Tr. Co. v. Grindle, 170 A.2d 280 (Del. 1961)
authorities_cited.proposition: Continuous use need not be constant, and temporary breaks do not destroy continuity absent intent to abandon; hostile use is shown by use to the exclusion of others without any declaration of intent.

authorities_cited.authority: Marvel v. Barley Mill Rd. Homes, 104 A.2d 908 (Del. Ch. 1954)
authorities_cited.proposition: Adverse possession creates a new legal title that is not lost by later cessation of possession; whether possession is open and notorious depends on the nature of the land and whether the possessor behaves as an owner would.

authorities_cited.authority: Acierno v. Goldstein, 2004 WL 1488673 (Del. Ch. June 25, 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: The true owner interrupts the possession period only by ousting the possessor, entering the property in a way that excludes the possessor.

authorities_cited.authority: Ayers v. Pave It, LLC, 2006 WL 2052377 (Del. Ch. July 11, 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: A hostile claim goes against the ownership claims of all others, including the record owner; preponderance burden.

authorities_cited.authority: Lisiewski v. Seidel, 899 A.2d 59 (Conn. App. Ct. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Common law courts award adverse possession title to only the portion of a parcel where the elements are satisfied.

authorities_cited.authority: HSBC Bank (USA) v. Nefedova, 2013 WL 6870025 (Mass. Land Ct. Dec. 31, 2013)
authorities_cited.proposition: An adverse possession claim was allowed in part and denied in part, with title awarded to a subsection of the disputed land.

authorities_cited.authority: DiGiacobbe v. Sestak, 743 A.2d 180 (Del. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: A master's factual and legal findings are reviewed de novo.

authorities_cited.authority: Acierno v. Goldstein, 2005 WL 3111993 (Del. Ch. Nov. 16, 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: The common law adverse possession claim is codified at 10 Del. C. § 7901.

authorities_cited.authority: Agilent Techs., Inc. v. Kirkland, 2010 WL 610725 (Del. Ch. Feb. 18, 2010)
authorities_cited.proposition: Preponderance means more likely than not.

authorities_cited.authority: Walker v. Five N. Corp., 2007 WL 2473278 (Del. Super. Aug. 31, 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: Quoted through Tumulty for the definitions of open and notorious and exclusive possession.

authorities_cited.authority: Mitchell v. Dorman, 2004 WL 117580 (Del. Ch. Jan. 16, 2004), aff'd, 860 A.2d 810 (Del. 2004) (TABLE)
authorities_cited.proposition: Quoted through Ayers for the definition of a hostile claim.

summary.brief_summary: The Murrays sued their self-represented neighbors, the Preradovics, to quiet title by adverse possession to a triangular strip of the Preradovics' lot. After trial, the Magistrate's final report recommended title only to the fenced-in portion and not to the adjoining stone planter and grass strip, and both sides took exceptions. Reviewing de novo and after a site visit, Chancellor McCormick held that subdivision is legally permissible under Justice v. McGinn but factually inappropriate here, because the planter and the retaining wall inside the fence form one contiguous feature with a shared drainage system. The Court found that the Murrays' consistent maintenance from 1998 to late 2022, without permission and without any use by the neighbors, satisfied every element of adverse possession for the whole area.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether, on de novo review of a Magistrate's post-trial final report, neighbors who proved adverse possession of a fenced-in triangular strip of the adjoining lot also acquired by adverse possession the unfenced remainder (a stone planter and a grass strip running to Halifax Road), or whether the disputed area should be subdivided and title to the unfenced portion denied.
summary.holding: The Murrays' exceptions are granted and the Preradovics' exceptions are denied, and judgment is entered for the Murrays on all issues. The Magistrate committed no legal error in subdividing the disputed land. The Court, however, had walked the property and found that the planter, retaining wall, fence and grass form one physically connected landscaping feature, so it declined to subdivide. It found that the Murrays proved each element as to the entire triangle. Possession was continuous for over twenty years from December 1998 through their own and their landscapers' maintenance, and occasional overgrowth did not break continuity. It was open and notorious because they maintained the features marking the practical boundary as any owner would. It was hostile and exclusive because they had no permission and no 234 South Dillwyn resident used or maintained the area before late 2022. Actual possession overlaps with open and notorious possession. The case is remanded to the Magistrate to implement an order defining the exact boundaries of the disputed area and awarding title over it to the Murrays.
key_facts_and_concessions: The planter outside the fence is made of the same stone as the retaining wall inside the fence, and the two share a drainage system; on the Court's site visit they appeared as "effectively one contiguous landscaping feature" extending into the grassy area.

Between 1998 and late 2022, the Murrays or people they hired were the only people to undertake maintenance or landscaping in the disputed area. That work included trimming ivy, planting in and removing vegetation from the planter, removing bamboo, trimming the Japanese Maple, and mowing. Martin Foster mowed and weed-whacked around the planter continuously, except in winter, from May 2007.
A 1998 Zebley & Associates inspection showed the fence encroaching nearly nine feet into 234 South Dillwyn, and a fence has stood in substantially the same location since at least December 1998.

Orth, Burkert and the Murrays all testified that they regarded the line formed by the fence and planter as the border between the properties; Orth believed the planter was on 23 Pinedale's property, and the Orths maintained grass only up to the back of the planter.
No resident of 234 South Dillwyn gave the Murrays permission to use the disputed area.

The only evidence against continuity was occasional overgrowth in and behind the planter. The Murrays credibly testified that they welcomed it as a privacy screen while still trimming the ivy and mowing. Some of the overgrowth came from trees behind the planter that the Murrays did not consider exclusively theirs.
The Preradovics first mowed and cut back vegetation in the planter in late 2022, after the twenty-year period had run.

The Murrays discovered that the Preradovics knew of the fence issue and had negotiated $3,000 off their purchase price. A later settlement under which the Murrays would buy the disputed area fell through and was held unenforceable.
summary.practical_takeaway: Where an adverse possession claim extends past a fence, build a record that the unfenced area is physically integrated with the enclosed area (shared materials or drainage) and that the claimant alone maintained it for the full twenty years, including landscaper payment records and testimony from prior owners on both sides. Because exceptions are reviewed de novo, consider requesting a site visit to show that integration firsthand.
summary.standard_of_review: De novo review of the Magistrate's factual and legal findings on exceptions (DiGiacobbe v. Sestak), with the record augmented by the Court's own site visit; Plaintiffs had to prove each element of adverse possession by a preponderance of the evidence.

entries.name: Aldercrest Health-Edmonds, LLC et al v. Salt Creek Beach, LLC et al

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Service never occurred because no signed green card was returned: rejected as a "counterfactual" and "litigation-driven" theory. Defendants cited no case law and did not refute Plaintiffs' authority. Under Applied Bank, certified mailing, delivery tracking and actual knowledge suffice, and a green card return is not required to perfect service (fn. 19).
Objection to Plaintiffs' requested remedy: waived. Defendants' opposition addressed only the lack-of-service argument and did not respond to Plaintiffs' remedy argument (fn. 25).

Failure to meet and confer: rejected (fn. 24). Unlike the Superior Court CCLD Rules, the Court of Chancery rules do not mandate meeting and conferring, though the Guidelines suggest it and best practice is for Delaware counsel to join the call. In any event, the emails attached to the Motion show the parties did meet and confer.
Removal to federal court tolled the response time: raised in correspondence but dropped in the opposition (fn. 13).

Complaint that Plaintiffs did not provide the green cards until their reply: called "nonsensical" because Defendants knew since July that discovery was outstanding and a green card is not required (fn. 19).

Good cause for failing to make timely objections to the requests for admission: none shown, and none could exist where Defendants recognized the need to respond, requested an extension and then did an "about-face" on service (fn. 27).

authorities_cited.authority: Applied Bank v. JHL Brighton Design and Décor Center, LLC, 2018 WL 501473 (Del. Super. Jan. 17, 2018)
authorities_cited.proposition: Service by certified mail was deemed perfected where no executed green card came back but the package was not returned, USPS tracking showed it was sent, and the defendant had actual knowledge of the suit.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 33(b)(3); Ct. Ch. R. 34(b); Ct. Ch. R. 36(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: Discovery served with the complaint must be answered within 45 rather than 30 days. Measured from July 20 delivery, responses were due September 3, 2026.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Delaware Public Schools Litig., 317 A.3d 251 (Del. Ch. 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: A party that fails to assert a proper, timely objection to a discovery request risks waiver of its objections; the same applies to requests for admission (n.51).

authorities_cited.authority: Bocock v. Innovate Corp., 2023 WL 8453525 (Del. Ch. Dec. 6, 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Deficient objections were held waived but privilege was preserved; the Court found Defendants' conduct more egregious and imposed the same remedy.

authorities_cited.authority: James Wm. Moore et al., Moore's Federal Practice § 36.11[5][c] (2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited through Delaware Public Schools: objections to requests for admission not raised in a timely objection are waived absent good cause.

authorities_cited.authority: Murphy v. State, 632 A.2d 1150 (Del. 1993)
authorities_cited.proposition: Failure to raise a legal issue in the text of the opening brief generally waives it.

authorities_cited.authority: Emerald Partners v. Berlin, 726 A.2d 1215 (Del. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: Issues not briefed are deemed waived.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 88
authorities_cited.proposition: Governs the fee submissions due within 14 days absent agreement.

authorities_cited.authority: Court of Chancery Guidelines (meet and confer)
authorities_cited.proposition: Parties "should" meet and confer before raising discovery disputes; this is a best practice, not a mandate under the Chancery rules.

authorities_cited.authority: Superior Court CCLD Rules
authorities_cited.proposition: Unlike the Chancery rules, they mandate a meet-and-confer requirement.

authorities_cited.authority: 10 Del. C. § 3104; Super. Ct. Civ. R. 4(f)
authorities_cited.proposition: The service procedures under which Applied Bank deemed service perfected.

authorities_cited.authority: Del. Const. art. IV § 13(2)
authorities_cited.proposition: Basis for Judge Adams sitting as a Vice Chancellor by designation.

summary.brief_summary: Plaintiffs Aldercrest Health-Edmonds, LLC et al. moved to compel discovery responses from Defendants Salt Creek Beach, LLC et al., who argued they were never served because no signed green return-receipt card came back from the certified mailing. Judge Adams, sitting as a Vice Chancellor by designation, rejected this "gamesmanship." Defendants had acknowledged the requests, asked for an extension, and only after taking it unilaterally raised a service defense; under Applied Bank, tracking and actual knowledge establish service without a returned green card. The Court ordered responses with all objections other than privilege waived, declined to deem the requests for admission admitted, and awarded fees and costs.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Defendants could avoid responding to discovery requests mailed by certified mail on the theory that service was never perfected because no signed green return-receipt card came back, where USPS tracking showed delivery and Defendants' counsel had acknowledged the requests and sought an extension to respond; and, if not, what sanction applied to the overdue responses.
summary.holding: Motion to compel granted. The Court found the discovery requests were properly served, consistent with Delaware caselaw, relying on certified mailing, USPS tracking showing July 20 delivery, the signed green cards and counsel's acknowledgment of the requests. Giving Defendants the benefit of the doubt, it set the response deadline at September 3, 2026, 45 days after July 20 delivery. Defendants waived any objection to the remedy by not addressing it. The Court ordered four remedies: (1) Defendants must produce all responsive documents within 30 days, with no objection other than privilege, or risk further sanctions; (2) if not already done, Defendants must give complete written interrogatory responses within 7 days of the order, with no objection other than privilege; (3) "in the interests of trying this case on the merits," the requests for admission are not deemed admitted, but complete written responses are due within 7 days, with no objection other than privilege; and (4) Plaintiffs are awarded reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, with Rule 88 submissions due within 14 days absent agreement, which the Court encouraged.
key_facts_and_concessions: Plaintiffs sent the discovery requests by Certified Mail, return receipt requested, on July 15, 2026. The Court personally reviewed USPS tracking showing each package "served on July 20, 2026 in Rocklin, CA", and Plaintiffs later produced green cards signed "D. Funk" showing receipt on July 20 (fn. 18-19).

Defendants' counsel discussed the outstanding discovery with Plaintiffs' counsel by phone on July 22 or 23. Defendants' counsel did not contradict the July 24 email memorializing that call, which noted the pending requests and stated, "I anticipate that discovery will be illuminating" (fn. 20).
By email on August 26, Defendants' counsel acknowledged the August 31 deadline and asked for an extension to September 11. Plaintiffs' counsel did not agree.
After September 11 passed and Plaintiffs' counsel followed up, Defense counsel first raised the theory that the discovery had not been properly served and so was not yet due.

In their opposition, Defendants represented they would serve responses on or before the October 28 hearing. They missed that self-imposed deadline, and responses were not filed until after the hearing.

Plaintiffs did not file the return of service until September 10. Plaintiffs' counsel represented at argument that filing it seemed unnecessary because Defendants had indicated they received the requests (fn. 5). The tracking numbers listed in the return for Cardiff Beach, LLC and Wailea Beach, LLC were erroneous (fn. 18).
The Complaint was served the same way, by Certified Mail, and Defendants never objected to that service (fn. 23).
Defendants removed the action to the District of Delaware on August 7, and it was voluntarily remanded on September 10.
summary.practical_takeaway: Once counsel has acknowledged discovery requests and sought an extension, do not later contest service of those requests or treat an unconsented extension as granted; serve timely objections, because missing the deadline without good cause risks waiver of everything but privilege, plus fees. Opposition briefs on a motion to compel should also address the requested remedy, since silence waives any objection to it.
summary.standard_of_review: Not stated (motion to compel; response deadlines under Ct. Ch. R. 33(b)(3), 34(b) and 36(a)).

entries.name: In re Illumina, Inc. Consolidated Derivative Stockholder Litigation

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Argument that the Court may not consider the post-closing ECJ Judgment: rejected. Caremark/Massey claims function as indemnification claims, and the ECJ did not change the law but held the EC never had jurisdiction. There was therefore no valid standstill for Illumina to violate.

Argument that Eagle Force Holdings v. Campbell requires treating the standstill like a status quo order violated while a jurisdictional challenge was pending: rejected. The EC is a regulator, not a court; the ECJ annulled its acts with retroactive effect; and the EU dispute concerned the EC's statutory authority under the EUMR, not personal jurisdiction.

Argument that dismissal would contradict the Court's July 16, 2024 bench ruling in the Pavers 220 Action, which said the standstill was positive law the board 'knowingly appears to have violated': rejected (fn. 133). Preliminary observations made on an expedited record under the credible-basis test do not bind the Court in the plenary action.

Argument that the closing violated the Clayton Act even absent a legal impediment or final ruling: rejected. No final determination of a violation exists, and the Court declined to expand its jurisdiction by adjudicating the Clayton Act to find Massey liability.

Argument that the FTC withdrew its injunction application on the assumption Illumina would honor the standstill: rejected. Knowing the FTC did not want the merger to close is 'a far cry' from a court order restricting closing.

Argument that demand futility should be measured by the board in place when the Omaha Police Action was filed in February 2024, ignoring later events: not preserved. Plaintiffs pleaded the Demand Board as of the Pavers filing in the designated operative complaint, and Defendants relied on that pleading.

Argument that the ruling lets fiduciaries 'pick and choose' which regulatory directives to follow, or lets later jurisdictional outcomes justify knowing violations: rejected. The argument wrongly assumes the law applied to Illumina and GRAIL at closing, and the Court expressly disclaimed creating either rule.

Reliance on Kandell v. Niv: rejected. Kandell involved a business model built on a clear violation of a federal regulation, whereas EU enforcement here rested on a new, untested interpretation. Kandell itself warned against liability where a regulator rejects a rationally compliant position.

Reliance on Lebanon County Employees' Retirement Fund v. Collis: rejected. Collis rested on a plethora of red flags (investigations, subpoenas, lawsuits) showing awareness of compliance deficiencies, and none exists here.

Futility as to Count II against deSouza: rejected (fn. 152). That theory depended on increasing the Director Defendants' exposure on Count I, and they face no substantial likelihood of liability on Count I.

authorities_cited.authority: United Food & Com. Workers Union & Participating Food Indus. Emps. Tri-State Pension Fund v. Zuckerberg, 262 A.3d 1034 (Del. 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: Three-part universal test for demand futility, applied director by director; demand is excused if at least half the demand board is compromised.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Massey Energy Co., 2011 WL 2176479 (Del. Ch. May 30, 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Fiduciaries cannot loyally cause a Delaware corporation to seek profit by knowingly violating the law; Massey's facts involved a recidivist record of violations.

authorities_cited.authority: In re TransUnion Deriv. S'holder Litig., 324 A.3d 869 (Del. Ch. 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Massey claim requires that the corporation broke the law, that fiduciaries purposely caused it to do so, and that they did so in pursuit of greater profits; Massey is not a claim separate from Caremark.

authorities_cited.authority: Firefighters' Pension Sys. of City of Kansas City v. Found. Bldg. Materials, Inc., 318 A.3d 1105 (Del. Ch. 2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Massey claim cannot be asserted preemptively; the Court typically requires a prior adjudication of violation, a fine or penalty, or a settlement.

authorities_cited.authority: South v. Baker, 62 A.3d 1 (Del. Ch. 2012)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Caremark claim operates as a tag-along indemnification action.

authorities_cited.authority: L.A. City Emps.' Ret. Sys. v. Sanford, 352 A.3d 276 (Del. Ch. 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Derivative suits are a form of indemnification claim that ripens when the triggering loss is established; plaintiffs must plead a substantial likelihood of Massey liability for a majority of the demand board.

authorities_cited.authority: Ont. Provincial Council of Carpenters' Pension Tr. Fund v. Walton, 2023 WL 3093500 (Del. Ch. Apr. 26, 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Bad faith under Massey requires an intentional decision to cause a violation of law. Its two lawyer-advice paradigms distinguish a protected business judgment made under some regulatory doubt from a conscious decision to stay out of compliance.

authorities_cited.authority: Melb. Mun. Firefighters' Pension Tr. Fund v. Jacobs, 2016 WL 4076369 (Del. Ch. Aug. 1, 2016)
authorities_cited.proposition: No bad faith where the board believed its conduct was lawful, appealed the regulatory findings and proclaimed the company's innocence.

authorities_cited.authority: Ritchie v. Baker, 2025 WL 2048014 (Del. Ch. July 22, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Massey is an extreme version of Caremark; corporate recovery absent fines or penalties for the alleged misconduct defies common sense; futility folds into the merits.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Plug Power Inc. S'holder Deriv. Litig., 2025 WL 1277166 (Del. Ch. May 2, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: The demand board is the one in place when claims are validly in litigation; an argument for a different demand board not pleaded in the amended complaint is not preserved; futility folds into the merits of the claim.

authorities_cited.authority: Asteris v. Commission of the European Communities (Apr. 26, 1988)
authorities_cited.proposition: An annulment by the EU court has retroactive effect.

authorities_cited.authority: AmerisourceBergen Corp. v. Lebanon Cty. Emps.' Ret. Fund, 243 A.3d 417 (Del. 2020)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Section 220 proceeding under the credible-basis test is not a merits assessment, so observations made there do not bind the plenary action.

authorities_cited.authority: Eagle Force Holdings, LLC v. Campbell, 187 A.3d 1209 (Del. 2018)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Delaware court may punish violations of its status quo order even if it later finds it lacked personal jurisdiction. Inapposite here because the EC is a regulator, its acts were annulled, and the dispute concerned statutory authority.

authorities_cited.authority: Kandell v. Niv, 2017 WL 4334149 (Del. Ch. Sep. 29, 2017)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Massey claim was sustained where the business model depended on a clear violation of CFTC Regulation 5.16; directors are not liable when a regulator rejects a rationally compliant position.

authorities_cited.authority: Lebanon Cty. Emps.' Ret. Fund v. Collis, 311 A.3d 773 (Del. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cited for intent to violate positive law as a loyalty breach and for limiting the futility analysis to what the demand board knew; distinguished because its reversal rested on a plethora of red flags absent here.

authorities_cited.authority: Brewer v. Turner, 2025 WL 2769895 (Del. Ch. Sep. 29, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: A Caremark claim was sustained where the general counsel had advised that a policy did not comply with federal regulation; no comparable advice was alleged here.

authorities_cited.authority: IBEW Loc. Union 481 Defined Contribution Plan & Tr. v. Winborne, 301 A.3d 596 (Del. Ch. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: Bad faith may be pleaded through scienter, meaning actual or constructive knowledge that the conduct was legally improper.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Caremark Int'l Inc. Deriv. Litig., 698 A.2d 959 (Del. Ch. 1996); Stone v. Ritter, 911 A.2d 362 (Del. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Oversight liability requires a sustained or systematic failure of oversight reflecting bad faith.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 23.1
authorities_cited.proposition: A derivative plaintiff must make demand or plead particularized facts showing futility.

authorities_cited.authority: Braddock v. Zimmerman, 906 A.2d 776 (Del. 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Demand is assessed as to the board in place when the claims are validly in litigation.

authorities_cited.authority: Aronson v. Lewis, 473 A.2d 805 (Del. 1984)
authorities_cited.proposition: Directors, not stockholders, manage the corporation's affairs.

authorities_cited.authority: Desimone v. Barrows, 924 A.2d 908 (Del. 2007)
authorities_cited.proposition: Directors have no authority knowingly to cause the corporation to become a rogue.

authorities_cited.authority: 15 U.S.C. § 18 (Clayton Act § 7)
authorities_cited.proposition: Prohibits acquisitions that may substantially lessen competition; the alleged U.S. law violation.

authorities_cited.authority: EUMR Articles 7 and 22
authorities_cited.proposition: The Article 22 referral mechanism and the Article 7 standstill (suspension) obligation.
Pavers obtained books and records before suing, and those documents were incorporated by reference.

authorities_cited.authority: Cent. Mortg. Co. v. Morgan Stanley Mortg. Cap. Hldgs. LLC, 27 A.3d 531 (Del. 2011)
authorities_cited.proposition: Rule 12(b)(6) reasonable-conceivability standard.

summary.brief_summary: Illumina stockholders derivatively sued Illumina's directors and former CEO deSouza, asserting a Massey loyalty claim for closing the GRAIL acquisition while an EC standstill was in effect and while the FTC was challenging the deal under Clayton Act § 7. Defendants moved to dismiss under Rules 23.1 and 12(b)(6), and Vice Chancellor Fioravanti granted dismissal with prejudice under Rule 23.1. The Court held that the ECJ's later ruling that the EC lacked jurisdiction meant no EU law was violated, and that no U.S. law was violated absent any bar to closing or final Clayton Act adjudication. A Board acting on extensive legal advice amid uncertain regulatory risk did not act in bad faith, so no Demand Board member faced a substantial likelihood of liability.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether demand on Illumina's board was excused under the Zuckerberg universal test, where plaintiffs' only futility theory was that a majority of the Demand Board faced a substantial likelihood of liability on a Massey claim for authorizing the August 2021 closing of the GRAIL merger. Plaintiffs said the closing violated (i) the EC's Article 7 EUMR standstill, imposed after an Article 22 referral that the ECJ later annulled for lack of EC jurisdiction, and (ii) Section 7 of the Clayton Act, although no court ever finally adjudicated a violation.
summary.holding: Motion granted under Rule 23.1, and the Amended Complaint is dismissed with prejudice; the Court resolved the case on the 'gating question of demand futility.' The Demand Board was fixed as of the Pavers filing on December 23, 2024, because plaintiffs pleaded it that way and did not preserve an earlier-board theory. No EU law was violated: the ECJ held that the EC never had jurisdiction, and annulment of the referrals (retroactive under EU law) meant the standstill never validly applied. The Court said it need not consider the EC's post-ECJ withdrawal decisions to reach that conclusion (fn. 139). No U.S. law was violated: no legal bar to closing existed, no final Clayton Act adjudication occurred, and the Court declined to adjudicate the Clayton Act itself. With no violation of positive law, plaintiffs could not plead bad faith. The minutes also showed an informed Board acting on counsel's advice that the EC lacked jurisdiction and that no U.S. barrier existed, while preserving compliance through hold-separate arrangements and continued litigation; that places the case in Walton's protected business-judgment paradigm. The Court did not reach Defendants' alternative 'legal risk' argument (fn. 130). Demand was also not futile as to Count II against deSouza, because that theory depended on Count I (fn. 152).
key_facts_and_concessions: The Board resolved on August 17, 2021 to close the merger while the EC standstill was in effect. It did so after advice from Cravath, Slaughter and May, Paul Hastings, Monckton Chambers and Covington. Monckton Chambers (with Slaughter and May concurring) advised that Illumina had strong arguments the EC lacked jurisdiction, though 'the EU court favors the EC agencies, making the outcome uncertain.'

On September 3, 2024 the ECJ held that the EC lacked jurisdiction over the merger and annulled the EC's acceptance of the member-state referral requests that triggered the standstill. The EC then withdrew all of its merger decisions, including the approximately €432 million fine, and described the withdrawal as ex tunc.

Plaintiffs acknowledged that the HSR waiting periods had expired and conceded that no U.S. court order barred closing. The FTC voluntarily withdrew its preliminary injunction application and imposed no fine.

No final Clayton Act determination exists. The ALJ ruled for the merger, the FTC Commissioners reversed, and the Fifth Circuit vacated and remanded for applying the wrong legal standard. Illumina divested GRAIL before the remand was heard.

Plaintiffs did not argue that any Demand Board member received a material personal benefit or lacked independence (fn. 125). Futility rested solely on substantial likelihood of liability for the seven Director Defendants on the eleven-member Demand Board.

The Amended Complaint, designated as the operative pleading by agreement in the consolidation, pleaded the Demand Board as the board in place when the Pavers Action was filed on December 23, 2024. It did not plead the board in place when the Omaha Police Action was filed in February 2024.

Counsel warned the Board of possible EC fines of up to 10% of annual revenues. The Board was also told the EC process could not finish before GRAIL could terminate after December 20, 2021, and was advised on the $300 million reverse break fee.

At closing the Board adopted Hold Separate Commitments, which ultimately cost $3.09 billion. It also continued the EU jurisdictional challenge and publicly committed to abide by the final EU and U.S. outcomes.
summary.practical_takeaway: A Massey claim premised on breach of a regulator's directive can fail outright if a court later holds the regulator lacked jurisdiction. Absent a prior adjudication, fine or settlement, the claim may also be unripe, and Section 220 bench observations will not carry the plenary case. Plaintiffs consolidating derivative actions should plead the demand board they intend to rely on in the designated operative complaint, because an earlier-board theory not pleaded there is not preserved.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 23.1 demand futility under United Food & Commercial Workers Union v. Zuckerberg, applied director by director. Plaintiffs needed particularized facts supporting a reasonable inference that at least six of eleven Demand Board members faced a substantial likelihood of liability. Because futility rested on the merits of the claim, the inquiry 'folds into' the strength of the underlying Massey claim. The Court also recited the Rule 12(b)(6) reasonable-conceivability standard but resolved the motion solely on Rule 23.1.
